stem: What is the average cell cycle span for a mammalian cell?
solution: About **24 hours**. Human cells in culture, which illustrate a typical eukaryotic cell cycle, divide once in approximately every 24 hours. Of this, cell division proper (**M phase**) lasts only about an hour, while **interphase** lasts more than 95% of the cycle. The duration varies from organism to organism and from cell type to cell type (yeast completes a cycle in about 90 minutes).
groundedIn: §10.1.1; Fig. 10.1 — human cells in culture divide once in approximately every 24 hours; M phase about an hour, interphase more than 95%; yeast about 90 minutes

stem: Distinguish cytokinesis from karyokinesis.
solution:
| Basis | Karyokinesis | Cytokinesis |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Division of the **nucleus**: separation of daughter chromosomes into two daughter nuclei | Division of the **cytoplasm**, separating the cell into two daughter cells |
| Sequence | Comes first; the M phase starts with it | Follows karyokinesis; cell division is completed at its end |
| Stages / mechanism | Four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase | A furrow in the plasma membrane in animal cells; a cell-plate in plant cells |
| Result | Two daughter nuclei | Two daughter cells, with organelles such as mitochondria and plastids distributed between them |

Karyokinesis can occur without cytokinesis: the result is a multinucleate condition, a **syncytium** (e.g., liquid endosperm in coconut).
groundedIn: §10.1.1; §10.2; §10.2.5 — M phase starts with karyokinesis and usually ends with cytokinesis; four stages of karyokinesis; furrow vs cell-plate; organelles distributed; syncytium in liquid endosperm of coconut

stem: Describe the events taking place during interphase.
solution:
**Interphase** is the phase between two successive M phases. Though called the resting phase, it is the time during which the cell prepares for division by undergoing both **cell growth** and **DNA replication** in an orderly manner. It lasts more than 95% of the cell cycle and is divided into three phases:

1. **G\(_1\) phase (Gap 1):** the interval between mitosis and the initiation of DNA replication. The cell is metabolically active and grows continuously but does not replicate its DNA.
2. **S phase (Synthesis):** DNA synthesis or replication takes place. The amount of DNA per cell doubles (2C to 4C), but the chromosome number does not increase (a 2n cell stays 2n). In animal cells the **centriole duplicates** in the cytoplasm.
3. **G\(_2\) phase (Gap 2):** **proteins are synthesised** in preparation for mitosis while cell growth continues.

Cells that do not divide further exit G\(_1\) and enter the inactive quiescent stage (G\(_0\)).
groundedIn: §10.1.1 — interphase is the resting phase in which the cell prepares by growth and DNA replication; G1, S, G2 events; 2C to 4C, chromosome number stays 2n; centriole duplicates; G0

stem: What is G\(_o\) (quiescent phase) of cell cycle?
solution:
The **quiescent stage (G\(_0\))** is an inactive stage which cells that do not divide further enter on exiting the **G\(_1\) phase**. Cells in this stage remain **metabolically active** but **no longer proliferate** unless called on to do so, depending on the requirement of the organism. Example: heart cells in adult animals do not appear to divide.

The question prints the subscript as the letter o; the stage is G-zero, G\(_0\), as the chapter writes it.
groundedIn: §10.1.1 — cells that do not divide further exit G1 to enter the quiescent stage (G0); metabolically active but no longer proliferate; heart cells

stem: Why is mitosis called equational division?
solution: Mitosis is called **equational division** because the **number of chromosomes in the parent and the progeny cells is the same**. At anaphase the centromere of each chromosome splits and the two sister chromatids move to opposite poles, so each daughter nucleus receives one complete set. A diploid cell therefore gives diploid daughter cells with an **identical genetic complement**.
groundedIn: §10.2; §10.2.3; §10.3 — since the number of chromosomes in parent and progeny is the same it is called equational division; chromatids separate to opposite poles; diploid daughter cells with identical genetic complement

context: Name the stage of cell cycle at which one of the following events occur:
stem: Chromosomes are moved to spindle equator.
solution: **Metaphase**: spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores, and the chromosomes are moved to the spindle equator and aligned along the metaphase plate.
groundedIn: §10.2.2 — chromosomes are moved to spindle equator and get aligned along metaphase plate

context: Name the stage of cell cycle at which one of the following events occur:
stem: Centromere splits and chromatids separate.
solution: **Anaphase** (of mitosis): centromeres split and the chromatids separate and move to opposite poles. The same event occurs at anaphase II of meiosis.
groundedIn: §10.2.3; §10.4.2 — anaphase: centromeres split and chromatids separate; anaphase II begins with splitting of the centromere

context: Name the stage of cell cycle at which one of the following events occur:
stem: Pairing between homologous chromosomes takes place.
solution: **Zygotene** of prophase I of meiosis: homologous chromosomes start pairing, a process called **synapsis**.
groundedIn: §10.4.1 — zygotene: chromosomes start pairing together; this association is called synapsis

context: Name the stage of cell cycle at which one of the following events occur:
stem: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes takes place.
solution: **Pachytene** of prophase I of meiosis: crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes at the recombination nodules.
groundedIn: §10.4.1 — pachytene: recombination nodules, the sites at which crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids

context:
Describe the following:
Draw a diagram to illustrate your answer.
stem: synapsis
solution:
**Synapsis** is the pairing (association) of **homologous chromosomes** during **zygotene**, the second stage of prophase I of meiosis.

1. It follows leptotene, during which the chromosomes become gradually visible and compact.
2. Electron micrographs show that synapsis is accompanied by the formation of a complex structure, the **synaptonemal complex**, between the paired chromosomes.
3. The complex formed by a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes is a **bivalent** (tetrad).
4. The synaptonemal complex dissolves at the beginning of diplotene.

**Diagram** (as in Figure 10.3, Prophase I): a cell in which each pair of homologous chromosomes lies side by side along its length. Labels: homologous chromosomes (one of each pair), sister chromatids, centromere, and the synaptonemal complex between the paired homologues.
groundedIn: §10.4.1; Fig. 10.3 — zygotene: chromosomes start pairing, called synapsis; synaptonemal complex; bivalent or tetrad; synaptonemal complex dissolves at diplotene

context:
Describe the following:
Draw a diagram to illustrate your answer.
stem: bivalent
solution:
A **bivalent** (or **tetrad**) is the complex formed by a **pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes** during zygotene of prophase I.

1. Each homologous chromosome has two sister chromatids, so a bivalent carries **four chromatids**.
2. The four chromatids become distinct and clearly appear as tetrads at **pachytene**, when crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids.
3. At diplotene the homologues of the bivalent tend to separate, remaining linked at the chiasmata.
4. At metaphase I the bivalents align on the equatorial plate; at anaphase I the homologous chromosomes of each bivalent separate.
5. A diploid (2n) cell forms n bivalents, one per pair of homologues.

**Diagram** (as in Figure 10.3, Prophase I): two homologous chromosomes paired side by side, each made of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. Labels: homologous chromosomes, sister chromatids, non-sister chromatids, centromere, the four chromatids of the tetrad.
groundedIn: §10.4.1; Fig. 10.3 — the complex formed by a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes is called a bivalent or a tetrad; four chromatids distinct at pachytene; bivalents align at metaphase I; homologues separate at anaphase I

context:
Describe the following:
Draw a diagram to illustrate your answer.
stem: chiasmata
solution:
**Chiasmata** (singular: chiasma) are the **X-shaped structures** seen at **diplotene** of prophase I, where the homologous chromosomes of a bivalent remain linked at the **sites of crossing over**.

1. At pachytene, crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes at the recombination nodules, and the chromosomes stay linked at those sites.
2. At the beginning of diplotene the synaptonemal complex dissolves and the recombined homologues tend to separate from each other **except at the sites of crossovers**; these points of contact are the chiasmata.
3. During diakinesis the chiasmata undergo **terminalisation**.
4. Chiasmata are thus the visible evidence of crossing over, which recombines genetic material.

**Diagram** (as in Figure 10.3, Prophase I): a bivalent whose two homologous chromosomes have moved apart along most of their length but cross each other at one or two X-shaped points. Labels: chiasma, non-sister chromatids, sister chromatids, centromere, homologous chromosomes.
groundedIn: §10.4.1; Fig. 10.3 — recombined homologues separate except at the sites of crossovers; these X-shaped structures are chiasmata; terminalisation of chiasmata in diakinesis

stem: How does cytokinesis in plant cells differ from that in animal cells?
solution:
| Basis | Animal cells | Plant cells |
|---|---|---|
| Reason for the difference | No cell wall; the plasma membrane can constrict | Enclosed by a relatively **inextensible cell wall** |
| Mechanism | Appearance of a **furrow** in the plasma membrane | Formation of a new cell wall starting with a **cell-plate** |
| Direction | The furrow gradually deepens from the periphery and joins in the centre | Wall formation starts in the **centre** of the cell and grows **outward** to meet the existing lateral walls |
| Structure formed | Only the plasma membrane divides the cytoplasm | The cell-plate, a simple precursor that represents the **middle lamella** between the walls of the two adjacent cells |

In both, organelles such as mitochondria and plastids are distributed between the two daughter cells.
groundedIn: §10.2.5; Fig. 10.2 — animal cell: furrow in plasma membrane deepens and joins in the centre; plant cells: inextensible cell wall, wall formation starts in the centre and grows outward, cell-plate represents the middle lamella

stem: Find examples where the four daughter cells from meiosis are equal in size and where they are found unequal in size.
solution:
Meiosis ends at telophase II with four haploid daughter cells; whether they are equal in size depends on whether the cytoplasm is divided equally at cytokinesis.

**Equal in size:**
1. **Spermatogenesis** in animals: the four haploid cells formed by meiosis develop into four sperms of equal size.
2. **Microsporogenesis** in flowering plants: a microspore mother cell forms a tetrad of four equal microspores (pollen grains).

**Unequal in size:**
1. **Oogenesis** in animals (e.g., humans): the cytoplasm is divided unequally, so meiosis gives one large **ovum** (egg) and small **polar bodies**.
groundedIn: §10.4; §10.4.2 — meiosis during gametogenesis forms haploid gametes; four haploid daughter cells at telophase II after cytokinesis; BEYOND CHAPTER: spermatogenesis gives four equal sperms; microsporogenesis gives a tetrad of four equal microspores; oogenesis divides the cytoplasm unequally, giving one large ovum and small polar bodies

stem: Distinguish anaphase of mitosis from anaphase I of meiosis.
solution:
| Basis | Anaphase of mitosis | Anaphase I of meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| What separates | **Sister chromatids** of each chromosome | **Homologous chromosomes** of each bivalent |
| Centromere | **Splits**; the chromatids become daughter chromosomes | **Does not split**; sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres |
| What moves to each pole | Single chromatids (daughter chromosomes) | Whole chromosomes, each with both its chromatids |
| Chromosome number at each pole | Same as the parent cell (2n in a diploid cell) | Half that of the parent cell (n) |
| Genetic make-up of the separating units | Sister chromatids identical | Chromatids of a chromosome may differ, because of crossing over at pachytene |
groundedIn: §10.2.3; §10.4; §10.4.1 — anaphase: centromeres split and chromatids separate; anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids remain associated at centromeres; meiosis halves the chromosome number; crossing over at pachytene

stem: List the main differences between mitosis and meiosis.
solution:
| Basis | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Cells in which it occurs | Diploid somatic cells in animals (haploid cells in a few, e.g., male honey bees); both haploid and diploid cells in plants | Specialised diploid cells that form gametes (gametogenesis) |
| Number of divisions | One nuclear division followed by one cytoplasmic division | Two sequential divisions, **meiosis I** and **meiosis II**, with only a single DNA replication |
| Daughter cells | **Two** | **Four** |
| Chromosome number | Same as the parent (**equational division**) | Reduced to **half**: haploid cells (reduction division) |
| Prophase | Short and simple | Prophase I long and complex, with five stages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis |
| Pairing of homologues | Absent | Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) to form bivalents |
| Crossing over | Absent | Occurs at pachytene between non-sister chromatids |
| Metaphase | Chromosomes align at the metaphase plate | Bivalents align at the equatorial plate in metaphase I |
| Anaphase | Centromeres split; sister chromatids separate | Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate, centromeres do not split (they split in anaphase II) |
| Genetic make-up of daughter cells | Identical to the parent | Varied, because of recombination |
| Significance | Growth, cell repair, restoring the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio | Conserves the chromosome number across generations; increases genetic variability |
groundedIn: §10.2; §10.3; §10.4; §10.4.1; §10.4.2; §10.5 — mitosis equational, diploid somatic cells, male honey bees, plants haploid and diploid; meiosis two divisions single replication, four haploid cells, prophase I five stages, synapsis, crossing over, metaphase I and anaphase I events; significance of each

stem: What is the significance of meiosis?
solution:
1. **Conservation of chromosome number:** meiosis is the mechanism by which the specific chromosome number of each species is conserved across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, even though it reduces the chromosome number by half.
2. **Formation of haploid gametes:** meiosis during gametogenesis produces haploid gametes and the haploid phase of the life cycle; fertilisation then restores the diploid phase.
3. **Genetic variability:** crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes at pachytene recombines genetic material, so meiosis increases genetic variability in the population from one generation to the next.
4. **Evolution:** these variations are very important for the process of evolution.
groundedIn: §10.5; §10.4; §10.4.1 — conservation of specific chromosome number across generations; haploid gametes and fertilisation restores diploid phase; crossing over recombines genetic material; increases genetic variability, important for evolution

stem: haploid insects and lower plants where cell-division occurs, and
solution:
Mitosis is usually restricted to diploid cells, but haploid cells divide by mitosis in some social insects and in some lower plants.

1. **Haploid insects:** **male honey bees** are haploid, and their cells divide by mitosis.
2. **Lower plants:** in **haplontic algae** such as Volvox and Spirogyra, the haploid plant body grows by mitosis; in **bryophytes** (mosses and liverworts) the dominant haploid gametophyte grows by mitosis and forms its gametes by mitosis; the haploid **prothallus** of ferns also grows by mitosis.
groundedIn: §10.1.1; §10.3 — haploid cells divide by mitosis in male honey bees; in some lower plants and some social insects haploid cells divide by mitosis; plants show mitosis in haploid and diploid cells; BEYOND CHAPTER: the haploid plant body of Volvox and Spirogyra, the gametophyte of mosses and liverworts and the fern prothallus grow by mitosis, and bryophyte gametes are formed by mitosis

stem: some haploid cells in higher plants where cell-division does not occur.
solution:
In flowering plants several haploid cells of the gametophytes do not divide further:

1. **Male gametes** formed in the pollen grain.
2. The **egg cell** of the embryo sac (it divides only after fertilisation, as the diploid zygote).
3. The **synergids** of the embryo sac.
4. **Three of the four megaspores** formed by meiosis of the megaspore mother cell, which degenerate.

Like cells that exit G\(_1\) and stop proliferating, these cells do not enter another cell cycle.
groundedIn: §10.1.1; §10.3 — plants show mitosis in haploid as well as diploid cells; cells that do not divide further exit G1; BEYOND CHAPTER: male gametes, the egg cell and the synergids of the embryo sac do not divide, and three of the four megaspores degenerate

stem: Can there be mitosis without DNA replication in 'S' phase?
solution:
**No.** Mitosis cannot take place without DNA replication in the S phase.

1. In the S phase the DNA per cell doubles (2C to 4C), so each chromosome comes to consist of **two sister chromatids** held together at the centromere.
2. At anaphase the centromere splits and one chromatid of each chromosome goes to each pole; this is how each daughter nucleus receives a complete set of chromosomes and 2C DNA.
3. Without replication, each chromosome would have only one chromatid and there would be nothing to separate; the daughter cells could not receive intact genomes. Cell division, DNA replication and cell growth are therefore coordinated so that progeny cells contain intact genomes.

Meiosis II, which resembles mitosis, follows interkinesis without any DNA replication; it is possible only because each chromosome still has the two sister chromatids made in the S phase before meiosis I.
groundedIn: §10.1; §10.1.1; §10.2.3; §10.4.1; §10.4.2 — processes coordinated to give progeny with intact genomes; S phase doubles DNA 2C to 4C; chromatids separate at anaphase; no DNA replication during interkinesis; meiosis II resembles mitosis

stem: Can there be DNA replication without cell division?
solution:
**Yes.**

1. **Syncytium:** in some organisms karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis. DNA replicates and the nucleus divides repeatedly, but the cell does not divide, giving a multinucleate condition (e.g., the **liquid endosperm in coconut**).
2. **Endoreduplication:** in some cells the DNA replicates repeatedly with no nuclear or cell division; the replicated strands stay together as giant **polytene chromosomes**, e.g., in the salivary gland cells of Drosophila.
groundedIn: §10.1.1; §10.2.5 — DNA replication occurs in S phase; karyokinesis not followed by cytokinesis gives a syncytium, e.g. liquid endosperm in coconut; BEYOND CHAPTER: endoreduplication producing polytene chromosomes in the salivary gland cells of Drosophila

context: Analyse the events during every stage of cell cycle and notice how the following two parameters change
stem: number of chromosomes (N) per cell
solution:
For a diploid cell with 2n chromosomes, the chromosome number stays **2n** through interphase and early mitosis, doubles to **4n** only at **anaphase**, and returns to **2n per cell** after cytokinesis.

| Stage | Chromosomes per cell | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| G\(_1\) | 2n | Diploid cell before replication |
| S | 2n | DNA doubles but the chromosome number does not increase |
| G\(_2\) | 2n | Each chromosome has two sister chromatids |
| Prophase | 2n | Chromosomes condense; each has two chromatids |
| Metaphase | 2n | Chromosomes align at the metaphase plate |
| Anaphase | 4n | Centromeres split; each chromatid is now a daughter chromosome |
| Telophase | 4n (2n in each of the two nuclei) | Nuclear envelope forms around each set |
| After cytokinesis | 2n in each daughter cell | Cytoplasm divides |

In meiosis the number falls to n per cell after meiosis I (homologues separate) and stays n after meiosis II.
groundedIn: §10.1.1; §10.2.1; §10.2.2; §10.2.3; §10.2.4; §10.2.5; §10.4.1 — chromosome number stays 2n after S phase; chromatids at prophase and metaphase; at anaphase daughter chromatids become daughter chromosomes; two daughter nuclei at telophase; cytokinesis; homologues separate in anaphase I

context: Analyse the events during every stage of cell cycle and notice how the following two parameters change
stem: amount of DNA content (C) per cell
solution:
Taking the DNA content after M phase as 2C, it **doubles to 4C in the S phase**, stays 4C through G\(_2\) and mitosis, and returns to **2C per cell** after cytokinesis.

| Stage | DNA content per cell | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| G\(_1\) | 2C | No DNA replication |
| S | 2C rising to 4C | DNA synthesis doubles the amount of DNA |
| G\(_2\) | 4C | Replication complete; proteins synthesised |
| Prophase | 4C | Each chromosome has two chromatids |
| Metaphase | 4C | Chromatids still joined at centromeres |
| Anaphase | 4C | Chromatids separate, but within the same cell |
| Telophase | 4C (2C in each of the two nuclei) | Two daughter nuclei form |
| After cytokinesis | 2C in each daughter cell | Cytoplasm divides |

In meiosis, the 4C cell gives 2C per cell after meiosis I and C per cell after meiosis II, since there is no replication during interkinesis.
groundedIn: §10.1.1; §10.2.3; §10.2.4; §10.2.5; §10.4.1; §10.4.2 — G1 no DNA replication; S phase 2C to 4C; G2 protein synthesis; chromatids separate at anaphase; two daughter nuclei; cytokinesis; no replication during interkinesis; four haploid cells
